queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the huge buttressed trunk, about 15 metres round, ringed by a protective platform. It stands on its own in a small gully of myrtle beech on the Ada Tree walk.
queue.story:
Measured for the National Trust in 1986, the Ada Tree stood 67 metres tall. An article from 1993, reproduced on the Trust's own register page, gives it 76, and another guide says 75.1. The honest answer is somewhere between the high sixties and the mid seventies.

The girth is less disputed: 15 metres round at a metre and a half above the ground by the Trust's figure, with the state heritage database reported at 15.5. Great buttress wings flare from the base, and a platform has been built around it so visitors stay off the roots.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the black park sign in front of it naming it the Giant Tree, national champion coast redwood. It stands on the Big Trees Loop by the Big Tree Area parking on Bull Creek.
queue.story:
In November 1991 the American Forestry Association named this coast redwood the national champion of its species, and the park's sign beside it still gives the figures. It is 363 feet tall, about 110 metres, with a trunk 53.2 feet round, about 16 metres, and an average crown spread of 62 feet. Save the Redwoods League explains that the title goes to the best combination of height, trunk and crown, not to height alone.

queue.name: Giant Tree

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by standing clear above the palm canopy of the Palm Grove, one of the tallest things in the garden. The pin marks a point among the palms, so look up.
queue.story:
The seed was picked on New Year's Day, 1849, at Maryborough in Queensland, by John Carne Bidwill, the first director of the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney. It went into the Palm Grove in 1853 and the tree that came up is still standing there, more than 170 years later, pushing well clear of the palm canopy around it as one of the tallest things in the garden.

It is the Garden's type specimen of Queensland kauri, the first of the species planted here, and other kauris in Sydney get measured against it. queue.tree_name: The Ginkgo of the United Order of Tents
queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the ginkgo in front of the United Order of Tents mansion, a house on a wide lot with a lawn with almost 100 feet of frontage. It stands at 87 MacDonough Street; look from the sidewalk.
queue.story:
For almost forty years New York's official list of its Great Trees did not change. In October 2024 NYC Parks finally reopened it, for the first time since 1985, adding 61 trees chosen from more than 270 nominations sent in by the public. This ginkgo in front of a mansion on MacDonough Street was one of them, and the house is the reason people put its name forward.

The mansion belongs to the United Order of Tents, a Black women's fraternal order that has served this community for more than 150 years and is said to have helped people escaping slavery. Coverage of the new list described the ginkgo as holding a piece of that history, which is about the best job description a front-yard tree can
queue.name: The Ginkgo of the United Order of Tents

queue.recognise: One of three Montezuma cypresses in the Rose Garden, west of the Rose Garden Tea Room and near the Queensland kauri, with soft, feathery foliage hanging in curtains.
queue.story:
The seed for this tree came from Mexico City. In 1912 William Hertrich, who built The Huntington's gardens, gathered Montezuma cypress seed in Chapultepec Park, possibly from El Sargento, a giant there that died in 1969 and whose fifty-foot trunk still stands. The Huntington now holds thirteen mature Montezuma cypresses, all grown from that collection: nine near the Lily Ponds and three here in the Rose Garden. In the garden's own telling, the Chapultepec trees go back to plantings made by the Mexica around 1450.

queue.name: The Huntington Montezuma Cypress

queue.tree_name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Blaise Castle
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, broad and flat-tiered in layers the way a Cedar of Lebanon grows. It stands near Blaise Castle House where Repton placed it, close to the children's playground.
queue.story: John Scandrett Harford, a wealthy Bristol banker, bought Blaise Castle Estate in 1789 and hired the two biggest names in English landscape design of the era, Humphry Repton and later John Nash, to remake it into a Picturesque parkland. Repton's method favoured framing views with carefully placed specimen trees rather than dense planting, and the Cedars of Lebanon he set out near Blaise Castle House are some of the estate's oldest surviving evidence of that design still growing where he placed it. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 7.5 metres round, under a crown 20.8 metres tall. It stands in Parque Marechal Carmona, which has more than one Moreton Bay fig; this is the one the state classified.
queue.story:
An Australian fig with a trunk seven and a half metres round grows in a park in Cascais, and Portugal has protected it since 1996. The forestry institute, the ICNF, lists it as a tree of public interest, declared in the official gazette on 28 November 1996, and the town of Cascais carries it on its own list of classified trees under the name árvore-da-borracha, the rubber tree.

The register's numbers do most of the talking. A girth of 7.5 metres, a height of 20.8 metres in a 2016 record, and an age of about 110 years at its last measurement. queue.tree_name: The Pepper Tree That Mended Nets
queue.recognise: You can recognise it in autumn and winter by clusters of small, bright red drupes hanging from an otherwise unremarkable street tree. It stands on Avenida Manuel Maria Portela.
queue.story: In a city built on sardines, this street tree used to work for the fleet. The parish records that the resin of the Brazilian pepper was used on fishing nets, a treatment that stiffened and waterproofed the fibres and slowed the rot that salt water works on anything organic. Setubal canned fish on an industrial scale from the nineteenth century onwards and the port is still the reason the city exists, so an ornamental avenue tree quietly feeding the tackle shed is a better fact than most trees on this page can offer. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 235 inches (about six metres) round, under a conifer 34 metres tall. It stands in the Huntington's Rose Garden, where it was named California's biggest Queensland kauri in 2021.
queue.story:
In 1908 a gardener cut through this tree's taproot and sealed the wound with a blowtorch. The tree was already 40 feet tall, and it lived.

The kauri had been planted in 1890 beside the Shorb family home. When Henry Huntington's mansion was going up, the tree stood in the way, and his master horticulturist William Hertrich chose to move it rather than fell it. Cutting the taproot freed it from the ground; the blowtorch was how he meant it to survive the move. More than a century on, it is the oldest planted tree on the Huntington's grounds.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque on its trunk, which says plainly that a storm shortened its crown soon after planting. It stands on the harbour side of the garden.
queue.story:
A plaque on the trunk explains that this tree will never reach the grandeur of the one it replaced, because a storm damaged its crown soon after it was planted. It is an unusually honest thing for a label to say, and it is accurate.

The original Wishing Tree was a Norfolk Island pine set out from a tub around 1816, under Elizabeth Macquarie's eye. By 1905 it was over thirty metres and the most popular tree in the Royal Botanic Garden, with a custom attached: three times around it forwards, three times backwards, and then make your wish. In the 1930s it was found to be dying of old age, and a replacement was bought with money raised by the Farmer's Children's Radio Birthday Club and planted
queue.name: The Wishing Tree

queue.tree_name: The Peruvian Pepper of the Jardim de Palhais
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its long, drooping leaves hanging almost to the ground, forming a green tent to stand under. It stands alone in the Jardim de Palhais, Sao Sebastiao.
queue.story: The Peruvian pepper is the weeping cousin of the tree on the avenue nearby, and the two together make a small lesson in how the same idea arrived in Europe twice. This one is Andean, it was carried back by the Spanish in the sixteenth century, and the Inca used its fruit for a fermented drink and its resin for embalming. What it looks like is a willow that took a wrong turn: long drooping compound leaves on branches that hang almost to the ground, so from underneath it forms a green tent. Crush a leaf and it smells sharply of pepper, which is the family trait, and in autumn it carries loose pink drupes on strings. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the broad trunk, 3.44 metres round, under a low crown only 14 metres tall. It stands on the lakeside path on the east shore of Roath Park Lake, almost opposite Lakeside Drive.
queue.story:
This oak was on the map before the park was. Ordnance Survey sheets of 1880 and 1900 both show an oak at this spot on the east side of what is now Roath Park Lake, so it was already growing when the marshland here was made into a park.

Cardiff's tree survey measured it in January 2015 at 3.44 metres round and only 14 metres tall, a short, broad tree rather than a tall one. From that girth the survey works out about 173 years on an average site, or about 157 on a good one, which puts its start somewhere between the early 1840s and the late 1850s. Add the years since, and it is roughly 170 to 190 years old now. That is an estimate from size, not a planting record.

queue.tree_name: The Grand Ginkgo of Goo Shrine
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by being the tallest thing on the grounds, 25 metres on a trunk 3.18 metres round, the largest of six ginkgos here. It stands north of the main hall, behind the stone boars at the gate.
queue.story:
The guardians at this shrine gate are wild boars rather than the usual stone lion-dogs, and the tree behind them is the tallest thing on the grounds. Kamigyo Ward measures the ginkgo standing north of the main hall at 25 metres, with a trunk 3.18 metres around, the largest of six sizeable ginkgos in the precinct. A Kyoto travel description puts the shrine's big ginkgos at several hundred years old. That is an estimate rather than a measured figure and nobody has narrowed it since, so several hundred years is as close as anyone can honestly get.

queue.name: The Grand Ginkgo of Goo Shrine

queue.recognise: A short, enormously thick oak in a clearing in the Furze Hill wood, its trunk covered in burrs and hollows, a few long limbs reaching out sideways, a low wooden rail and a green bench nearby.
queue.story:
In 2014 England held its first Tree of the Year vote, and this squat Essex oak lost to Sherwood's Major Oak, the most famous tree in the country, by 465 votes. Its own website gives a trunk about 9.5 metres round on a tree just 4.3 metres high, and calls it 800 years old; others say 600, maybe 800. Either way it has the shape of a very old oak that has lost most of its height and kept its girth.

The name describes it. The trunk is a mass of burrs, lumps and hollows, and a few long limbs reach out sideways from a short, broken top. A wildlife writer who walked here with a group saw elephants, a moose and a stag in them.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the double row of giant redwoods lining the original drive just inside the garden entrance. It is the first thing visitors walk through, so you cannot miss it.
queue.story:
An American planted this avenue of giant sequoias in 1863, a year after he bought the estate. James Piers Patrick lined the original drive to Benmore House with them, from seed William Lobb had brought to Britain, and more than 160 years later they are the first thing you walk through at Benmore Botanic Garden. They stand around 50 metres tall now, by the garden's own figure.

They are not well. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, which runs Benmore, says the crowns are thinning, the lower branches have lost their needles and the soil beneath them is compacted. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its huge hollow trunk, about 12.5m round, ringed by a post-and-wire fence and interpretive signage beside the road. It stands on Derby-Gibb River Road, near Myall's Bore.
queue.story:
The prison in the name looks like a fiction. Historians Kristyn Harman and Elizabeth Grant, and separately the anthropologist Kim Akerman, traced the story of Aboriginal prisoners held inside this hollow boab back to a 1948 newspaper description of an artwork, and to a different, similarly named tree at Wyndham. No evidence has turned up that anyone was ever locked in this trunk.

What is documented is older and quieter. In 1916 the anthropologist Herbert Basedow photographed it as a living boab used by Aboriginal people as a shelter and a burial place, and recorded bleached human bones inside it. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by being the tallest tree in the park, a Californian giant sequoia about 34 metres high. It stands on the same lawn as Cantonspark's dawn redwood, a fifteen minute walk from Baarn station.
queue.story:
The tallest thing in this village park is a Californian. A giant sequoia, 5.20 metres around and roughly 34 metres tall when it was last measured in 2014, standing a fifteen minute walk from Baarn station and a long way from the Sierra Nevada, where the species survives in a scatter of groves and nowhere else in the wild.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted, so the age here is an estimate rather than a record. The park was laid out from 1902 for the industrialist August Janssen, passed to Utrecht University in 1918, and the university added a pinetum, a teaching collection of conifers, for its botany students. A girth of 5.20 metres fits a tree put in the ground somewhere in that window.
queue.name: The Cantonspark Giant Sequoia
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the enormous burl bulging from its southern face and the fire scar on its western side. It stands on the Congress Trail, about 140 feet uphill from the President.
queue.story:
This tree is named for the man who gave the Cherokee a written language. Sequoyah finished his syllabary in 1821, and a century later one of the largest trees in the Giant Forest was given his name.

Park superintendent Colonel John R. White gave it the name in the 1920s. One source says 1926 and another 1928, and neither has corrected the other, so both years stay here. The sources also disagree slightly on where it ranks: 27th largest giant sequoia in the world by one count, 30th by another, and ninth largest in the Giant Forest itself. The quarrel is about places on a list, not about scale. The trunk is roughly 27.5 metres round at the base and the tree stands close to 70 metres tall.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its huge, deeply fissured cork trunk (4.15m round) under a wide spreading crown, ringed by a small protective fence. It stands beside a playground and benches in the village of Aguas de Moura.
queue.story:
A single stripping of this tree in 1991 produced more than 1,200 kilos of cork, reportedly enough to stopper over 100,000 bottles of wine. Most cork oaks do not manage that in a whole lifetime. This one has been harvested more than twenty times since around 1820 and is still working.

It is called the Whistler for the noise. Songbirds gather in the crown at dusk and the sound carries down the street. Guinness lists it as the largest cork oak in the world, and in 2018 it won European Tree of the Year on 26,606 public votes, beating the ancient elms of Cabeza del Buey in Spain by a little over four thousand.

queue.recognise: A lone, broad oak at the edge of a ploughed field by the SP50, a short straight trunk under a round crown as wide as it is tall, with nothing else of its size in sight.
queue.story:
Out on the flat farmland of the Ferrara plain, where the provincial road to Poggio Renatico runs past the farm called Possessione Malvasta, one pedunculate oak stands alone at the edge of a ploughed field. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists it there: 461 centimetres round and 23 metres tall.

Nothing else of its size stands anywhere near it, and it has the shape of a tree grown in the open, with a short straight trunk and a crown as wide as it is tall, branching low on every side.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the dark red sap running from a broken stub on its trunk. It is the second yew on the right of the avenue leading to the church door at St Brynach's.
queue.story:
The second yew on the right as you walk up to St Brynach's church weeps a dark red-brown sap from a broken stub, and thousands of people come every year to see it. The Ancient Yew Group is blunt about the avenue it stands in. These yews are of no great age, it says, and are on its list only because of the bleeding one.

Why it bleeds is the question the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park asks on its own page about the tree, along with when it will stop. Legend has its answers. One links it to the Crucifixion. Another says it will bleed until a Welsh prince rules again from Nevern Castle, on the hill above the village.

queue.recognise: You can recognise them by the trunks standing in the water itself, with the cypress knees breaking the surface around them. They grow calf deep in the pond in front of the Palacio de Cristal, not on the bank beside it.
queue.story: Several bald cypresses grow directly out of the pond in front of the Palacio de Cristal, their trunks and lower roots permanently submerged, a planting scheme that only works because this particular conifer, unlike almost every other cone-bearing tree, tolerates and even prefers standing water. Bald cypresses develop distinctive above-water root growths called pneumatophores, sometimes called cypress knees, that let the roots breathe oxygen the flooded soil cannot supply, an adaptation evolved in the swamps of the southeastern United States rather than anywhere near Madrid. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trail: Trolleken is the veteran oak on the waymarked Trollskogsstigen, the 4.5-kilometre path from Naturum Trollskogen, and at 800 to 900 years it is the oldest oak on Öland.
queue.story:
Öland's oldest oak is somewhere between 800 and 900 years old, and nobody has ever published how thick it is.

Trolleken stands on the Trollskogsstigen, a 4.5-kilometre marked trail through Trollskogen, the troll forest at the northeastern tip of the island. The reserve dates only from 1998 and covers 266 hectares, with a visitor centre, a cafe and four waymarked trails, and it is one of the most visited places on Öland. The tree predates all of it by eight centuries.

queue.recognise: The single olive tree standing directly in front of the Ajuntament building on Placa de Cort, its wide low crown and thick multi-stemmed trunk unmistakable against the square's stone facades.
queue.story:
This olive is older than the square it stands in, and it has only been standing there since 1989. It grew for centuries at Pedruixella Petit, an estate near Pollenca with about two thousand olive trees, until a city gardener and the head of public works came to its owner, the hotelier Jaime Batle, and asked to buy it for the town hall square. Batle refused to sell. When he learned where it would go, he gave it away instead.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk and branches clipped into the shape of a sailing ship, bow pointed west. It stands beside the Kyoko-chi pond at Kinkaku-ji.
queue.story: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the shogun who built the Golden Pavilion, once kept this tree as a bonsai in a pot. Sometime after Yoshimitsu's death in 1408, his potted pine was planted in the ground beside Kinkaku-ji's Kyoko-chi pond and trained into the shape of a sailing ship, its trunk and branches clipped over generations to suggest a hull, a mast and a bow pointed deliberately west, toward the Buddhist Pure Land. The result, Rikushu-no-matsu, land boat pine, has been maintained in that same nautical silhouette for roughly six centuries, making it one of the longest continuously shaped ornamental pines in Japan and one of the three trees Kyoto names among its most celebrated. queue.tree_name: The Ombu of the Essaouira Medina
queue.recognise: Fills a walled café courtyard in the medina: a broad smooth dome of trunk and root behind a low rope rail, a dozen grey stems rising from it into a crown over the tables.
queue.story:
"Oldest tree in Morocco inside the ombu cafe," wrote the reader who sent this photograph from the medina of Essaouira, with a GPS fix taken at its foot.

The tree is an ombu, Phytolacca dioica, a native of the South American pampas, and the photograph shows why people stop for one. Its trunk does not so much rise from the ground as pour out over it, a broad smooth dome of root and wood ringed by a low rope rail. Out of that dome a dozen grey stems climb into a crown that fills the whole courtyard and leans over the whitewashed walls, and the café's tables stand around its edge in the shade.
